summary: Methods of collecting information about a system, qualitative and quantitative analysis, comparing alternative solutions and writing system requirements.

blocks.content: During **analysis**, the analyst collects information about how the current system works and what users need.

blocks.title: The four main methods
rows: Many people at low cost; anonymous so answers may be honest; quick to analyse (closed questions)
Low response rate; questions cannot be explained; limited depth — no follow-up
Detailed answers; follow-up questions; analyst can explain questions
Time-consuming and expensive; few people; interviewee may not be honest; not anonymous
See what really happens; reliable first-hand information
People may behave differently when watched; time-consuming; may miss rare events
Shows data used (forms, reports, invoices); quick to understand inputs/outputs
Documents may be out of date or incomplete; does not show opinions

blocks.title: Choosing a method
blocks.content:
- 600 students' opinions about the canteen → **questionnaire** (many people, cheap).
- The school director's needs for a new report → **interview** (one key person, detail needed).
- How librarians actually issue books → **observation**.
- What data appears on current library cards → **examining documents**.

Questions often ask for disadvantages of questionnaires *and* interviews separately — make sure each answer refers to **that** method (e.g. interview: "time-consuming, so only a few people can be interviewed").

rows: Finding themes and patterns in answers
Objective, easy to compare and graph, large samples
Rich detail; explains reasons and motives
Subjective, harder to analyse, small samples
"72% of users wait more than 5 minutes"

theory.title: Using data collection to develop a new system

blocks.title: From collected data to a requirement
items: Decide **what you need to know** (inputs, outputs, processes, problems, users' needs).
Choose suitable **methods** for each group of people.
Collect the data (questionnaire, interviews, observation, documents).
**Analyse** it — count closed answers (quantitative) and group open answers into themes (qualitative).
Identify the **problems** of the current system and the **needs** of users.
Write the **requirements specification** for the new system.

blocks.content: There is usually more than one way to solve a problem, e.g. buy off-the-shelf software, have bespoke software written, or improve the paper system. The analyst compares them against criteria.

blocks.title: Example: a new booking system for a sports centre
Feasibility
blocks.content: Alternatives are judged on **technical** (can it be built?), **economic** (cost vs benefit), **legal**, **operational** (will users use it?) and **schedule** (time) feasibility.
A list of what the new system **must do** and **the conditions** it must meet, agreed with the client. It is used to design the system and later to evaluate it.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.content: What the system must **do**. "The system must allow teachers to add and delete student records." "The system must email a weekly report to parents."

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.content: **How well** it must work: performance, security, usability, reliability. "A search must return results within 2 seconds." "Only staff with a password can edit marks."

items.title: Hardware and software requirements
items.content: What is needed to run it: "Runs on Android 10 or later", "Needs 4 GB RAM".

blocks.title: Requirements from a scenario
blocks.content:
*Scenario: teachers record homework and achievement manually and want an app to share results with students and parents.*
1. The app must allow teachers to **add, edit and delete** student records.
2. The app must allow teachers to **assign homework** to a class.
3. The app must **send results** to students and parents automatically.
4. The app must keep data **secure** — each user logs in with a password.
Requirements must be **specific and testable** and must come from the scenario. "The app should be good" earns nothing; "The app must allow teachers to send announcements to parents" does.
